claims.statement: Schmandt-Besserat interprets Near Eastern token shapes and counts as accounting representations connected to later writing.

citations.locator: Before Writing: Accounting with Tokens, ca. 7500–3350 BC
citations.note: Read the shapes/goods correspondence and the distinction between number of tokens and kind of goods.

claims.note: Attributed archaeological interpretation; invented triangle/disc exercise is not presented as an excavated record.

claims.statement: Uruk administrative tablets and later phonetic uses of signs illustrate changes in what written records could express.

citations.locator: The Origins of Writing, paragraphs on Uruk administration, complexity of origins, and rebus principle; object captions ca. 3100–2900 BCE
citations.note: Inspected museum narrative and approximate object dates.

claims.note: No single birthday for writing or universal progression to alphabets is claimed.

claims.statement: A placeholder, zero as a number, its name and its notation have distinct histories; Indian work includes Brahmagupta’s seventh-century rules.

citations.locator: A history of Zero, opening distinctions and Brahmagupta arithmetic rules
citations.note: Read placeholder/number distinction, Babylonian notation and Indian arithmetic discussion.

claims.note: No unique inventor or first-ever date is assigned; modern division argument is explanatory, not attributed to Brahmagupta.

examples.scope: Original token record, positional-value examples and arithmetic answers only; not historical verification.

limitations: Selective Near Eastern and numerical history; not a worldwide writing survey or a date for the origin of speech.
Archaeological interpretation is attributed; modern codes and arithmetic are teaching examples, not ancient transcriptions.
